objections_raised: Novelty can be manipulative or destructive
Divine memory cannot be empirically verified

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Conceptual analysis, phenomenological description, analogical reasoning, theological reflection

philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Qualified optimism - redemption is possible but not guaranteed, and requires ethical responsibility
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Temporal perishing, aesthetic value, ritual, poetry, divine memory, redemption

structural_organization.structure_type: Thesis-antithesis-synthesis with successive refinements; each section restates and extends the previous argument

summary_of_core_decisions: The text argues that aesthetic emergence—the composition of inherited elements into novel patterns of felt significance—provides a model for redeeming temporal perishing without denying temporality. It develops this through a dialectic that moves from Whitehead's account of perishing to the problem of value preservation, then to aesthetic emergence as a solution, and then to further tensions (subjective/objective, secular/theological) and qualifications. The method is conceptual analysis grounded in process metaphysics, using examples from art and ritual to illustrate abstract claims. The conclusion is that redemption is relational and processual, not escape from time, and that it carries ethical obligations.
